reference.source: Rutherford's Vascular Surgery and Endovascular Therapy / Braunwald's Heart Disease
clinicalPearls: A bulbous outpouching at the origin of an aberrant subclavian artery, representing a remnant of the embryonic aortic arch
Most often accompanies an aberrant right subclavian artery arising from a left arch, or an aberrant left subclavian arising from a right arch
Together with the aberrant vessel it may complete a vascular ring that encircles and compresses the trachea and oesophagus
Frequently asymptomatic and found incidentally, but can cause dysphagia (classically dysphagia lusoria), stridor, cough, or chest and back discomfort
Cross-sectional CT or MR angiography defines the arch anatomy, the diverticulum size, and any airway or oesophageal compression
The diverticulum is prone to aneurysmal enlargement and carries a risk of dissection or rupture, which guides the threshold for repair
Symptomatic compression or significant aneurysmal change is treated by surgical or endovascular repair with revascularisation of the involved subclavian artery
reference.pathophysiology: Kommerell diverticulum is a congenital anomaly of aortic arch development in which failure of normal regression of a segment of the embryonic dorsal aorta leaves a saccular dilatation at the base of an aberrant subclavian artery. The aberrant vessel typically courses behind the oesophagus, and the diverticulum with its associated ligamentum arteriosum can complete a vascular ring encircling the trachea and oesophagus. Compression of these structures produces respiratory and swallowing symptoms, while the diverticulum wall, being structurally abnormal, is predisposed to progressive aneurysmal dilatation with attendant risks of dissection and rupture. Symptoms therefore stem from two mechanisms: mechanical compression of adjacent airway and oesophagus, and the consequences of aneurysmal degeneration of the diverticulum itself.
additionalDifferentials: Double aortic arch or other complete vascular ring
Thoracic aortic aneurysm of other cause
Oesophageal or mediastinal mass causing dysphagia
Achalasia or other primary oesophageal dysmotility
additionalInvestigations: CT angiography of the thoracic aorta to define arch anatomy and diverticulum dimensions
MR angiography as a radiation-free alternative for anatomy and surveillance
Barium swallow to demonstrate posterior oesophageal indentation in dysphagia lusoria
Echocardiography to assess associated congenital cardiac anomalies
Bronchoscopy or oesophagoscopy where airway or luminal compression is suspected
Pulmonary function or airway assessment when respiratory compression is present
redFlags: Rapid diverticulum enlargement or signs of dissection or rupture
Progressive stridor or respiratory compromise from airway compression
Severe or worsening dysphagia with weight loss
Acute severe chest or back pain suggesting an aortic emergency
reference.prognosis: Small asymptomatic diverticula may remain stable and can be monitored, whereas symptomatic or enlarging lesions carry a meaningful risk of complications, including dissection and rupture. Elective repair of appropriately selected lesions has good outcomes and relieves compressive symptoms.
pitfalls: Dismissing an incidental diverticulum without characterising its size or growth potential
Attributing dysphagia to a primary oesophageal disorder and missing a vascular ring
Underestimating the aneurysmal and rupture risk of the abnormal diverticulum wall
Failing to plan subclavian revascularisation when repairing the aberrant vessel
Overlooking associated arch or congenital cardiac anomalies
references: Rutherford's Vascular Surgery and Endovascular Therapy
